newsitem.title: HONG KONG: New HK securities law unlikely before handover.
newsitem.headline: New HK securities law unlikely before handover.

text.p: A securities and futures bill designed to update Hong Kong's trading laws is unlikely to be put to the legislature before the territory returns to Chinese rule, a Financial Services Branch official said on Wednesday.

"We had planned to slot this in sometime in February but since we have not come to a conclusion on the form or the substance of the final bill, it is premature to say when we can introduce the bill into the legislative council," said John Wan, Principal Assistant Secretary (Securities).

Hong Kong's securities and futures watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), issued the draft proposal in December and it had been hoped the bill would be submitted to the legislation process early this year.
"If we miss this slot then we would have to bid for a new slot and in other words we would have to compete with other branches of the government," said Wan.

Asked if the legislation could go through before Hong Kong is handed back to China on midnight of June 30 this year, Wan said: "It's a mammoth exercise and it simply cannot be completed in that sort of timeframe."
The draft Composite Securities and Futures Bill was drawn up after consultation between the SFC and members of the financial industry between April and mid-November last year.

It consolidates and updates eight existing laws under one cover, unifying terminology and taking into account changes that have occured in securities and futures markets in Hong Kong over the past 20 years.
"There is a working group formed to study the proposals together with the SFC and we are now working on it," said Wan.
"We are talking about 400 pages of material. There are 250 clauses, eight schedules, and they are supposed to repeal eight ordinances altogether with over 530 clauses or sections," he said.
He said many questions had been raised concerning the draft proposal and the SFC was revising it. Officials at the SFC were not immediately available to comment.
The South China Morning Post said on Wednesday the draft legislation would not be tabled in the Legislative Council this month "because it is too controversial in its present form".
Wan said the proposals involved "far reaching implications".
"There are new procedures introduced and there are new powers and changes of things," he said.
